lessons.title: Study Session 1: Why Every Life Has Purpose

blocks.text: Introduction In Course 1 you came to know yourself honestly, your patterns, your personality, your emotions, your confidence and your self-esteem, and you closed that course with an authenticity statement describing the woman you are becoming. This course, Designed for Purpose, asks the next question: becoming for what? Not every woman will lead a nation, found an organisation or stand on a public stage, and WODDI wants you to hear clearly, at the start of this course, that none of those things are what make a life purposeful. Purpose, as WNNN teaches it, is the meaningful direction every woman can walk in, expressed through the responsibilities she carries, the contribution she makes, and how faithfully she uses the one life she has been given, not something reserved for the few who become famous or celebrated. This study session opens the door to that direction.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: 14. Explain purpose as a meaningful direction expressed through responsibility, contribution and faithful use of one's life. 15. Recognise dignity and possibility within your own life circumstances, whatever they currently look like. 16. Identify needs around you that you are equipped to address. 17. Treat present responsibilities as preparation rather than as delay or distraction from purpose. 18. Distinguish genuine purpose from fame, a single job title or one dramatic discovery.
Main Content
From Identity to Purpose

Everything you built in Course 1, honest self-knowledge, an understanding of your personality, emotional awareness, comparison-free confidence and healthy self-esteem, was never meant to end in self- understanding alone. It was meant to prepare you to ask a bigger question: what is this self for? Purpose is where identity turns outward, toward the people and needs around you, without losing the ground you have already built within.
What Purpose Means

Purpose, in this course, is a meaningful direction expressed through responsibility, contribution and faithful use of your life. It is a direction you walk in, visible in how you carry your responsibilities today, rather than a single destination you arrive at once and finish. This definition frees you from a common and painful misunderstanding, that purpose must be discovered in one dramatic moment, usually described as a calling, a vision or a sudden clarity that some women

report and others never seem to receive. WODDI wants you to know that purpose more commonly unfolds gradually, through attention, faithfulness and repeated small evidence, the way a woman's own strength unfolds, rather than through a single revelation you either receive or lack. The psychiatrist Viktor Frankl, writing from his experience surviving Nazi concentration camps, argued in Man's Search for Meaning (1946) that the drive to find meaning, not merely pleasure or power, is the primary motivating force in human life, and that meaning is found through responsibility to something or someone beyond oneself, a claim that closely matches this study session's own teaching. Developmental psychologist William Damon's research on purpose among young people (Damon, 2008) similarly found that a clear sense of purpose was one of the strongest predictors of thriving among adolescents and young adults, more so than self-esteem or achievement alone, and that purpose typically develops through gradual engagement with real responsibility rather than sudden realisation.
Three Practices for Recognising Purpose

Dignity and Possibility in Your Life Wherever you are starting from, a rural community, a displaced or diaspora setting, a low-income household, a season of unemployment or study, recognising dignity and possibility in your own life is the first practice of this study session. Purpose is available to be discovered and lived from wherever you currently stand; it is not the reward given to women who begin with advantage. Needs You Are Equipped to Address Purpose commonly begins to show itself at the intersection of two things: a real need in the world around you, and something in you capable of meeting it. Looking honestly for needs you are equipped to address, in your family, your community, your workplace or your studies, is more productive than waiting for a need to announce itself dramatically. Present Responsibilities as Preparation Faith, a young woman in Lusaka, is currently caring for her younger siblings while completing her studies, and has come to feel this season is simply something to survive before her real purpose can begin. Treating present responsibilities as part of preparation, rather than as an obstacle to purpose, means recognising that the patience, organisation and care she is building now are not wasted years; they are formation for whatever she is being prepared to carry next.
Key Practices for Recognising Purpose
•   Recognise dignity and possibility in your life. •   Look for needs you are equipped to address. •   Treat present responsibilities as part of preparation.
Purpose Beyond Fame or a Single Title

Purpose is not limited to fame, a single job title or one dramatic discovery. A woman who quietly and excellently raises children of strong character is walking in purpose. A woman who faithfully keeps the books of a small community organisation is walking in purpose. A woman who becomes a well-known advocate on a national stage may also be walking in purpose, but visibility is not what makes any of these women purposeful; faithfulness to what has been placed in front of them is.

This matters because a narrow, celebrity-shaped idea of purpose quietly discourages far more women than it inspires. If you have been waiting to feel purposeful until your life looks a certain way publicly, WODDI is releasing you from that wait today. Frankl (1946) made a related point directly relevant here: meaning, in his research and clinical observation, was found at least as often in ordinary faithfulness and unseen effort as in dramatic achievement, and often more reliably so.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned that purpose is a meaningful direction expressed through responsibility, contribution and faithful use of your life, not a single dramatic discovery reserved for the visible or the famous. You practised recognising dignity and possibility in your own life, identifying needs you are equipped to address, and treating present responsibilities as preparation. This prepares you for Study Session 2, where you will begin identifying the specific gifts you bring to that purpose.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 19. What responsibilities or needs repeatedly draw my attention? 20. Where have I been waiting for my life to look a certain way before believing I have purpose? 21. Name one present responsibility you now see differently, as preparation rather than delay. Practical Output: Practical Output A timeline of moments when you felt useful, deeply concerned or strongly motivated to contribute.
References and Further Reading

•   Warren, R. (2002). The Purpose Driven Life. Grand Rapids: Zondervan. •   Garcia, H. and Miralles, F. (2016). Ikigai: The Japanese Secret to a Long and Happy Life. London: Hutchinson. •   Frankl, V. E. (1946). Man's Search for Meaning. Vienna: Verlag für Jugend und Volk.

Introduction Study Session 1 gave purpose a shape: a meaningful direction expressed through responsibility, contribution and faithful use of your life. This study session makes that direction concrete by turning your attention to your gifts, the specific abilities and capacities you bring, that can be developed and used in service to others. Many women carry gifts they have never named, either because the gift came so naturally it seemed unremarkable, or because no one around them ever pointed it out. WNNN wants you to look at yourself the way a wise woman looks at a garden she did not plant but has been entrusted to tend: with curiosity, attention, and a readiness to cultivate what is already growing there.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: 22. Explain gifts as abilities, capacities or ways of contributing that can be developed and used in service. 23. Notice abilities you learn quickly or perform naturally. 24. Use repeated feedback from others as evidence of a gift. 25. Test a suspected gift through real responsibility rather than assumption alone. 26. Explain why a gift becomes valuable through discipline, humility and ethical use rather than admiration alone.
Main Content
From Direction to Ability

Purpose gives you a direction to walk in. Gifts give you something specific to walk with. This study session focuses on gifts as abilities, capacities or ways of contributing that can be developed and used in service, the raw material purpose will eventually be expressed through.
What Gifts Are

A gift, in this study session, is not limited to performance talent, singing, public speaking or the abilities that draw an audience. Gifts include organisation, listening, patience with detail, the ability to comfort someone in distress, quick numerical reasoning, the ability to explain a difficult idea simply, and countless other ordinary-seeming capacities that quietly meet real needs. One reason many women underestimate their own gifts is that a gift, when it belongs to you, rarely feels remarkable. It feels obvious, easy, almost too simple to count. This is precisely why the practices in this study session lean on evidence and outside feedback rather than your own private sense of what is special; a gift is often clearest to the people who benefit from it, not to the woman who carries it.

Gallup researchers Donald Clifton and Marcus Buckingham (2001) built a research programme around a related claim: that people grow far more through developing their natural talents into strengths than through trying to fix their weaknesses, and that most people can name their own greatest talent only with real difficulty, precisely because it feels too natural to notice. The idea that ability takes many forms beyond academic or verbal skill is also supported by Howard Gardner's theory of multiple intelligences (1983), which identified distinct forms of ability, including interpersonal, spatial and bodily-kinesthetic intelligence, challenging any narrow definition of gift limited to what can be measured on a written test.
Three Practices for Discovering Your Gifts

What You Learn Quickly or Do Naturally Notice the skills or subjects that come to you with less struggle than they seem to cost others, not because you have not worked at them, but because something in you meets them halfway. This ease is one signal, though not the only one, of a gift worth developing further. Repeated Positive Feedback A single compliment proves little. A comment that keeps returning, from different people, in different settings, over time, is far more reliable evidence. If three separate people, unprompted, have told you that you explain things clearly, that pattern is worth taking seriously. Testing Abilities Through Real Responsibility Nomvula, in a township outside Johannesburg, is repeatedly asked, almost without being formally appointed, to coordinate events, gatherings and logistics within her community. She has never named this as a gift, assuming everyone finds this manageable. Accepting the next such responsibility deliberately, and paying attention to how it goes, tests the suspected gift against reality rather than leaving it as an untested assumption.
Key Practices for Discovering Your Gifts
•   Notice what you learn quickly or do naturally. •   Review repeated positive feedback. •   Test abilities through real responsibility.
Gifts Become Valuable Through Discipline, Not Admiration

A gift becomes valuable through discipline, humility and ethical use, not admiration alone. A woman with a natural gift for persuasive speaking who never disciplines that gift with truthfulness can become dangerous rather than useful. A woman with a natural gift for organisation who never holds it with humility can become controlling rather than helpful. This is why WNNN places gift discovery inside Blueprint Academy's larger formation, after the identity work of Course 1, rather than teaching gifts in isolation as a talent inventory. A gift without character becomes a liability to the very people it was meant to serve; a gift joined to the self-knowledge, values and integrity this Academy is building becomes genuinely useful. Clifton and Buckingham's research (2001) reaches the same conclusion from a different direction: strengths-based development consistently outperforms weakness-focused correction, but only where the
strength is also matched with sound character and ethical use, a qualification their later writing was careful to add.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to identify your gifts through what you learn quickly, repeated feedback from others, and real-world testing, and you learned that a gift becomes valuable through discipline and humility rather than admiration alone. This prepares you for Study Session 3, where you will learn to distinguish raw talent from developed, dependable strength.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 27. Which gift have I neglected because it seemed ordinary to me? 28. What repeated feedback have I received from others that I have not yet taken seriously? 29. Describe a responsibility that tested one of your gifts, and what you learned from how it went. Practical Output: Practical Output Ask three trusted people to identify two gifts they see in you, and compare their feedback with your own observations.
References and Further Reading

•   Buckingham, M. and Clifton, D. O. (2001). Now, Discover Your Strengths. New York: Free Press. •   Gallup CliftonStrengths Assessment, as a widely used, non-diagnostic strengths-identification instrument. •   Gardner, H. (1983). Frames of Mind: The Theory of Multiple Intelligences. New York: Basic Books. •   Romans 12:6, as an optional values-based reading on differing gifts. •   Qur'an 16:71 (Surah An-Nahl), as an optional values-based reading on differing gifts and provision.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

Introduction Study Session 2 helped you begin naming your gifts. This study session asks a sharper question: which of those gifts can you actually depend on? Not every natural talent has yet become a dependable strength, and knowing the difference protects you from two common mistakes, overestimating an untrained talent, and undervaluing a strength you have already quietly built through years of practice. WODDI is preparing you not merely to feel gifted, but to become dependable, the kind of woman whose ability shows up consistently, under pressure, whether or not she feels inspired that day.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: 30. Distinguish between raw talent, developed strength, knowledge and dependable competence. 31. Identify talents in your own life that still require training before they can be relied on. 32. Practise deliberately and seek feedback to convert talent into strength. 33. Connect your strengths to real outcomes and needs rather than leaving them abstract. 34. Explain why relying on raw talent alone produces inconsistency.
Main Content
From Naming to Depending

Study Session 2 helped you notice and name your gifts. This study session moves from noticing to depending, examining the difference between raw talent, developed strength, knowledge and dependable competence, so that you know not only what you carry, but how reliable it currently is.
Four Different Things Often Confused as One

Raw talent is a natural inclination or ease, present before any deliberate work has been done on it. Developed strength is that same inclination refined through repeated, deliberate practice. Knowledge is understanding gained through study, information about a subject rather than skill in performing it. Dependable competence is the point at which an ability can be trusted to show up reliably, under real conditions, including pressure, fatigue or an audience. These four are easy to confuse because they can look similar from the outside. A woman with raw talent and a woman with dependable competence may both perform well on a good day. The difference only becomes visible on a difficult day, when talent alone often falters and developed competence continues to hold. The clearest research on how talent becomes dependable strength comes from psychologist K. Anders Ericsson's decades of study on expert performance (Ericsson and Pool, 2016), which found that expertise across fields as different as music, chess and surgery was built not by raw talent alone but by deliberate

practice, a specific kind of effortful, feedback-driven repetition aimed at a clear weakness, sustained over years. It is worth noting that the popular claim requiring a fixed number of practice hours before mastery, sometimes summarised from Malcolm Gladwell's Outliers (2008), oversimplifies Ericsson's own research; what matters most is the quality and deliberateness of practice, not a specific hour count.
Three Practices for Building Strength from Talent

Talents That Require Training Some abilities you notice in yourself are genuinely raw, present but undeveloped. Identifying talents that still require training, honestly, without either dismissing them or assuming they are already strengths, is the first step toward building genuine strength rather than an inflated sense of ability. Deliberate Practice and Feedback Practising deliberately and seeking feedback means more than simply repeating an activity. It means practising with attention to what specifically needs improvement, and inviting correction from someone whose judgement you trust, rather than only repeating what already feels comfortable. Connecting Strength to Real Outcomes Grace, who lives with a physical disability and gets around using a wheelchair, has spent two years in Kampala deliberately developing her skill in public facilitation, seeking feedback after every session and adjusting accordingly. Connecting that strength to real outcomes and needs means she now looks for actual community, workplace or ministry settings where dependable facilitation is genuinely needed, rather than treating the strength as a private accomplishment with nowhere to be used.
Key Practices for Building Strength from Talent
•   Identify talents that require training. •   Practise deliberately and seek feedback. •   Connect strengths to real outcomes and needs.
Why Talent Alone Produces Inconsistency

Relying only on talent can produce inconsistency; strengths are built through repeated quality practice. A woman who trusts only her natural ease with a subject or skill will perform unpredictably, strong when conditions favour her, unreliable when they do not. This inconsistency is not a character flaw; it is simply the natural limit of talent that has not yet been disciplined into strength. This is worth remembering with compassion toward yourself. If an ability you thought you had let you down recently, under pressure or in an unfamiliar setting, this may not mean the talent was never real. It may simply mean the deliberate practice this study session describes has not yet been done. Ericsson's research (Ericsson and Pool, 2016) directly challenges the popular idea that talent alone predicts achievement, supporting this study session's own caution that talent without disciplined practice produces inconsistency rather than dependable strength.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to distinguish raw talent, developed strength, knowledge and dependable competence, and you practised identifying talents needing training, practising deliberately with feedback, and connecting strength to real outcomes. This prepares you for Study Session 4, where you will examine the difference between passion and the wider responsibility of purpose.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 35. Which talent needs disciplined development before I can depend on it? 36. Describe a recent situation where a natural ability let me down under pressure, and what that revealed. 37. Name one strength you have already built through repeated, deliberate practice. Practical Output: Practical Output A strengths inventory with evidence, current level and the next development action for each strength.
References and Further Reading

•   Ericsson, A. and Pool, R. (2016). Peak: Secrets from the New Science of Expertise. Boston: Houghton Mifflin Harcourt. •   Gladwell, M. (2008). Outliers: The Story of Success. New York: Little, Brown and Company. •   Gallup CliftonStrengths Assessment, as a widely used, non-diagnostic strengths-identification instrument.

blocks.text: Introduction You have now named your gifts and begun distinguishing your raw talents from your dependable strengths. This study session addresses a question many young women wrestle with quietly: should I follow my passion? WODDI's answer is more careful than a simple yes or no. Passion is real, and it matters. But passion, on its own, is an unreliable guide for an entire life, because passion changes with seasons, moods and circumstances in ways that purpose, rightly understood, does not need to.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: 38. Explain passion as strong interest or energy, and purpose as a wider responsibility that may include work that is difficult or unseen. 39. Use passion as a source of energy rather than the only basis for decisions. 40. Test an interest against your values, real needs and actual ability. 41. Remain open to purpose being expressed through several different roles or seasons. 42. Explain why purpose should be held with humility rather than certainty.
Main Content
A Question Many Women Ask Quietly

Should I follow my passion, or should I be practical? This study session does not force you to choose one over the other. Instead, it asks you to understand what each one is actually for, so that passion can serve your purpose instead of competing with it.
What Passion Is, and What Purpose Is

Passion is strong interest or energy, the pull you feel toward a subject, activity or cause. Purpose is a wider responsibility that may include work that is difficult or unseen, work that does not always feel exciting, and is not always applauded, but still matters. The confusion between the two causes real harm when a woman assumes that if something does not excite her, it cannot be part of her purpose, or conversely, that whatever excites her most today must automatically be her life's calling. Both assumptions collapse feeling and responsibility into one, and both leave a woman disoriented when her feelings inevitably shift. Computer scientist and author Cal Newport (2012) directly challenged what he calls the passion hypothesis, the popular advice to simply follow your passion, arguing from research and interviews that career satisfaction more reliably follows from developing rare and valuable skill first, with passion often growing afterward as competence and contribution grow. Psychologist Angela Duckworth's research on
grit (2016) adds a related finding: that sustained achievement across long timeframes depends on passion combined with perseverance through difficulty, not passion alone.
Three Practices for Distinguishing Passion and Purpose

Passion as Energy, Not the Only Decision-Maker Passion is valuable fuel. It sustains effort through long seasons of unseen work. But fuel is not the same as direction; a car with a full tank still needs someone deciding where it is going. Using passion as energy, not the only decision-maker, means letting it strengthen your purpose without letting it be the sole test of whether something is worth doing. Testing Interest Against Values, Needs and Ability An interest becomes trustworthy as a direction once it has been tested against three further questions: does it align with your values, does it meet a real need, and do you have, or can you develop, the ability it requires. An interest that fails all three tests may remain a hobby, worth enjoying, without needing to carry the weight of your entire purpose. Purpose Across Several Roles or Seasons Halima was deeply passionate about early childhood education in her twenties, teaching in a community school in Freetown. In her forties, she found her deepest sense of contribution had shifted to policy advocacy for children's welfare instead of direct teaching. Her purpose, service to children's wellbeing, did not change. Its expression moved through different roles as her season, capacity and opportunity changed. Remaining open to purpose expressed through several roles protects you from mistaking one chapter for the whole book.
Key Practices for Distinguishing Passion and Purpose
•   Use passion as energy, not the only decision-maker. •   Test interests against values, needs and ability. •   Remain open to purpose expressed through several roles or seasons.
Holding Purpose With Humility

Passion can change; purpose should be held with humility and reviewed through experience, counsel and results. This is not a weakness in your purpose; it is honesty about how understanding actually grows. A woman who claims total certainty about her purpose at twenty and refuses to ever revisit that claim is usually protecting her pride rather than protecting her purpose. Held with humility, purpose becomes something you can keep testing against real evidence, your actual results, the honest counsel of people you trust, and the needs still in front of you, rather than a fixed idea you must defend regardless of what life shows you. Duckworth's research (2016) suggests genuine passion is proven over years, including through the seasons that do not feel exciting; a woman who expects passion to remove all difficulty from her purpose has misunderstood both concepts.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to distinguish passion as energy from purpose as a wider responsibility, to test interests against values, needs and ability, and to hold purpose with humility as it is expressed across different roles and seasons. This prepares you for Study Session 5, where you will translate purpose into the daily priorities and habits of an intentional life.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 43. What do I still care about when recognition, excitement or convenience is removed? 44. Where have I confused a passing interest with my whole purpose, or dismissed a real responsibility because it did not excite me? 45. Describe one piece of work that is difficult or unseen, and how it might still connect to a wider purpose. Practical Output: Practical Output A comparison of three passions using a purpose filter: values alignment, real need, capacity, sustainability and potential contribution.
References and Further Reading

•   Newport, C. (2012). So Good They Can't Ignore You. New York: Grand Central Publishing. •   Duckworth, A. (2016). Grit: The Power of Passion and Perseverance. New York: Scribner. •   Ecclesiastes 3:1, as an optional values-based reading on seasons and purpose. •   Qur'an 94:5-6 (Surah Ash-Sharh), as an optional values-based reading on ease following hardship, across life's seasons.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

Introduction You now have language for your purpose, your gifts, your strengths and the difference between passion and responsibility. This study session brings all of it down to the level of an ordinary week, because purpose that never touches your calendar remains an idea rather than a life. Living intentionally does not mean living rigidly, and it does not mean having no room left for rest, family or the unplanned needs of people you love. It means your priorities, habits and relationships are chosen with your direction in mind, rather than simply accumulating by default.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: 46. Explain intentional living as choosing priorities, habits and relationships that support a meaningful direction. 47. Define a small number of current priorities. 48. Protect time for what matters most. 49. Review your choices regularly and correct drift when it appears. 50. Explain why intentional living must remain flexible for care, emergencies and changing circumstances.
Main Content
From Direction to a Daily Life

Purpose, gifts and strength mean little if they never shape an ordinary Tuesday. This study session focuses on choosing priorities, habits and relationships that support a meaningful direction instead of living only by pressure or impulse, translating everything built so far in this course into the actual texture of your week.
What Intentional Living Means

Intentional living is the practice of choosing, rather than merely reacting. Most days offer a woman far more demands than she can meet, requests, notifications, obligations and opportunities, all arriving with their own urgency. Without intentional priorities, a woman's time is quietly claimed by whoever or whatever shouts loudest, rather than by what she has actually decided matters most. This is not a call to control every minute. It is a call to notice the difference between a life built by decision and a life built by default, and to move deliberately toward the first. Stephen Covey's influential framework in The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989) distinguishes activities by two dimensions, urgency and importance, and argues that most people's time is quietly
consumed by what is urgent rather than by what is important, unless priorities are deliberately protected, a distinction directly reflected in this study session's own key practices.
Three Practices for Living Intentionally

Defining a Few Priorities A woman who tries to prioritise everything has, in practice, prioritised nothing. Defining a small number of current priorities, few enough to actually hold in mind and protect, is more useful than a long list that quietly becomes background noise. Protecting Time for What Matters Priorities that are never protected in your actual schedule remain wishes rather than commitments. Protecting time for what matters means treating that time with the same seriousness you would give an appointment with someone you respect, because it is, in fact, an appointment with your own purpose. Reviewing and Correcting Drift Patience, a widow raising three children in Accra, set a priority to invest weekly time in mentoring a younger woman in her community, and found, three months later, that the meetings had quietly stopped without any decision to end them. This is drift, not failure, and every intentional life experiences it. Reviewing choices and correcting drift regularly, weekly or monthly, is what keeps a good intention from silently disappearing.
Key Practices for Living Intentionally
•   Define a small number of current priorities. •   Protect time for what matters. •   Review choices and correct drift regularly.
Intentional, Not Rigid

Intentional living must remain flexible enough for care, emergencies, learning and changing circumstances. A woman whose intentional plan collapses at the first sick child, unexpected bill or family emergency has built rigidity, not intentionality. Real intentional living bends without breaking; it absorbs the unplanned and returns to its priorities once the emergency has passed, rather than treating every disruption as failure. This flexibility matters especially for women balancing study, work, caregiving and community responsibility at once, which describes a great many WNNN members. Intentionality is a discipline available to every woman, adjusted to the actual shape of her season, not the privilege of women with uncomplicated lives. More recent habit research by James Clear (2018) adds a practical mechanism for how intentional living becomes automatic over time, arguing that identity-based habits, built around the question of who you are becoming rather than only what you want to achieve, are more durable than habits built on willpower alone. Read alongside Course 1's work on authentic identity, this suggests that intentional living becomes easier, not harder, once it is anchored to the woman you already know yourself to be.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to translate purpose into an intentional life by defining a few priorities, protecting time for what matters, and reviewing and correcting drift, while remaining flexible for the unplanned demands of real life. This prepares you for Study Session 6, where you will draw everything from this course together into one personal purpose statement.

Reflect and Grow — Self-Assessment 51. Which current habit consumes time without serving my values or direction? 52. Where have I noticed drift in a priority I once cared about, and what caused it? 53. Name one boundary I need to protect in order to give my true priorities real time. Practical Output: Practical Output An ideal week designed to reflect your present purpose priorities, responsibilities and rest.
References and Further Reading

•   Covey, S. R. (1989). The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People. New York: Simon and Schuster. •   Clear, J. (2018). Atomic Habits. New York: Avery. •   Proverbs 16:9, as an optional values-based reading on planning and direction. •   Hadith, narrated in Jami' at-Tirmidhi, on tying one's camel and trusting God, an optional values-based reading on planning and direction.
Evidence to keep Keep a written note, worksheet, reflection or practical output from this study session. Your progress should show real learning before the quiz.

lessons.title: Study Session 6: Creating Your Personal Purpose Statement

blocks.text: Introduction You have walked through five study sessions: recognising that every life has purpose, discovering your gifts, distinguishing talent from dependable strength, separating passion from purpose, and choosing to live intentionally. This final study session does not add a new idea. It asks you to gather everything into one place: a concise working statement that connects your identity, your values, your gifts, the people you serve, and the contribution you intend to make. This is not a slogan for a wall or a line for a biography. It is a compass you will return to, in Course 3 and beyond, whenever the direction of your life needs to be checked against what you actually meant to build.
Learning Outcomes

By the end of this study session, you should be able to: 54. Explain a purpose statement as a concise working statement connecting identity, values, gifts, people served and desired contribution. 55. Write a purpose statement in clear language you personally understand. 56. Make the statement broad enough to remain true across different seasons of life. 57. Translate the statement into present, specific action. 58. Integrate the outcomes of Study Sessions 1 to 5 into one coherent statement of purpose.
Main Content
Bringing Five Study Sessions Together

Study Session 1 gave you a definition of purpose. Study Session 2 gave you your gifts. Study Session 3 gave you the difference between talent and dependable strength. Study Session 4 gave you the difference between passion and purpose. Study Session 5 gave you the practice of intentional living. This study session is where all five meet, in one concise, working purpose statement.
What a Purpose Statement Is

A personal purpose statement is a concise working statement that connects your identity, your values, your gifts, the people you serve, and your desired contribution. It answers, in a sentence or two, a question this whole course has been building toward: who are you, what do you carry, who is it for, and what difference is it meant to make. Notice the word working: this is a working draft, not a legal document or an irreversible vow. It is the best current expression of your direction, written honestly enough to guide real decisions, and humble enough to be refined as Study Session 4 already taught you purpose should be. Organisational researcher Simon Sinek (2009) popularised the practice of starting with why, the underlying purpose or belief driving an individual or organisation, arguing that decisions and

communication anchored in a clear why are more resilient and more motivating than those anchored only in what is done or how it is done. A personal purpose statement, as taught in this study session, is essentially Sinek's why applied to an individual life rather than an organisation.
Three Practices for Creating Your Purpose Statement

Clear, Personal Language Write in clear language you understand, not language borrowed to sound impressive. A purpose statement filled with words you would never actually say out loud to a friend will not survive contact with a hard week; it needs to be language that is genuinely yours. Broad Enough for Different Seasons Remember Halima from Study Session 4, whose purpose remained constant while its expression moved from teaching to policy advocacy. Making the statement broad enough for different seasons means writing toward the underlying contribution, rather than locking the statement to one job title that a future season might outgrow. Translating the Statement into Present Action A purpose statement that stays only on paper has not yet done its work. Translating the statement into present action means identifying two or three specific things you can begin doing now, this month, that visibly express the statement, so that it becomes something you live rather than something you merely wrote.
Key Practices for Creating Your Purpose Statement
•   Write in clear language you understand. •   Make the statement broad enough for different seasons. •   Translate the statement into present action.
A Compass, Not a Prediction

A purpose statement is a compass, not a prediction; it may be refined as understanding grows. You are not being asked to forecast your entire future in one sentence. You are being asked to write down, honestly and as clearly as you can today, the direction you intend to walk in, knowing that a compass is meant to be consulted again and again, not written once and forgotten. Damon's research on purpose (2008) found that the clearest, most sustaining purpose statements were revisited and refined across a person's life as experience deepened, precisely the compass, not prediction, principle this study session has already taught you.
Closing This Course

Designed for Purpose began by asking why every life has purpose, and it closes with your own answer written in your own words. You now carry a working purpose statement, tested against your identified gifts, your dependable strengths, your honest separation of passion from responsibility, and your intentional daily choices. This is the direction WODDI has been helping you clarify: not fame, not a single title, but a life faithfully aimed at meaningful contribution.

Carry this purpose statement forward into Course 3, Rooted in Values, where you will examine the values that will keep this direction steady under pressure, and into every course that follows across Blueprint Academy. The woman who knew herself in Course 1, and who now knows her direction through Course 2, is the same woman who keeps walking, becoming more, becoming ready.
Study Session Summary and Conclusion

In this study session, you learned to write a personal purpose statement connecting your identity, values, gifts, people served and desired contribution, in clear language, broad enough for different seasons, and translated into present action. You learned to hold it as a compass rather than a fixed prediction. This closes Course 2 and prepares you for Course 3, Rooted in Values.
